did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title attributes it to Asaph, and it opens with the words, “A song, a psalm.”
Did you know? At the beginning of the psalm, there is a threefold appeal to God not to remain silent: “Do not be silent,” “Do not be quiet,” and “Do not be still.”
Did you know? The enemies are described as conspiring in secret against the people called “those you protect”—the people under God’s protection.
Did you know? The enemies’ goal is stated explicitly: to destroy Israel so that its name as a nation will be remembered no more.
Did you know? The psalm lists a broad coalition of nations, including Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek.
Did you know? Assyria is described as joining the enemies’ alliance and serving as “an arm for the descendants of Lot.”
Did you know? The poet recalls the defeat of Midian and the defeat of Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon River as examples of victories from the past.
Did you know? The leaders of Midian mentioned in the psalm include Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna; the poet asks that the enemy leaders suffer a fate like theirs.
Did you know? The enemies are compared to a rolling tumbleweed and to chaff before the wind—images that emphasize scattering and instability.
Did you know? The psalm concludes by stating the purpose of God’s intervention: that everyone may know that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth.
